VSL Merch Concepts R2

Round 2. The twelve pieces you kept, pushed further, plus three replacements for the ones you cut: a straight-edge tally longsleeve, a 5 a.m. reflective longsleeve, and the board rack. No eyebrows on the garments or on this page. Specs and 50-unit costs live in the notes beside each sheet.

How to review: tap In or Out on each piece. Every bullet in the notes (phrase candidates, alternates, colorways, risks) has its own ✓ and ✗, so approve or kill options line by line. Then Copy marks and paste the list in the chat.

StreetwearPerformanceObjectsNeo-WesternLatino

Streetwear

Salt Lake is for the weird

Lane thesis (unchanged): Salt Lake is for the weird. Band-merch logic: back prints, sleeve hits, xerox texture, one-line phrases, the straight-edge X as hardware, SLC Punk! blue-black-white.

What changed from R1 under the CD's rule: the sheet header, the spec strip and every small tracked-caps line are gone. Sheets are now lookbook pages: the piece name set large, two plain sentences, the garment, the graphic blown up, swatches with names, a short caption. The spec lives here. The only small type left on any garment is the flyer bar on piece 02 ("ALL AGES" / "NO RE-ENTRY" in typewriter inside inverse bars, tilted and pasted up like 31-flickr-flyer-c), which is a flyer device, not a label, and the handwritten "actual size" on its back, which is a marker note with an arrow. If Yid reads either as an eyebrow, both come off without hurting the piece.

Palette: Ink #212121, Cream #F6F1EC, Salt Pink #F58B88. Off-palette hit: Poster Blue #1A3BD4 on piece 03 only. Fonts in the SVGs are stand-ins (Anton for condensed poster type, Permanent Marker for hand lettering, Special Elite for typewriter); all text is live vector text. Each sheet is 1200 x 1500 and self-contained.

01 801, COUNTED IN X's (tally longsleeve, replacement for the cut All Ages piece)

File: 01-801-tally-longsleeve.svg

IN references: 04-online-ceramics-slaughterhouse-longsleeve.jpg (XXX stack down a black sleeve, white ink), 19-flickr-straight-edge.jpg (the X'd hand, the scene's hardware), 01-online-ceramics-grateful-60-longsleeve.jpg (a count as the whole graphic), 03-online-ceramics-blink182-dude-ranch-longsleeve.jpg (sleeve print plus a small chest hit).

Idea: A black longsleeve whose back is a tally of straight-edge X's that counts to 801, the area code, the way you count on a wall: four X's and a strike, 160 full groups and one X left over. The lone 801st X is the chest hit; the wearer's left sleeve says "801" in marker, the right sleeve is the XXX. No venue list, no band, no words beyond the number.

Why this over the other two options: the zine-collage back and the xerox photo tee both need licensed 1990s photographs, and the approved set has none we can clear. The tally needs nothing but a marker and a letterer, and it is the most band-merch object of the three: a sleeve-and-back shirt that only makes sense if you know what an X on a hand means.

Garment and fabric: 6.5 to 7 oz heavyweight longsleeve (Shaka Wear or Los Angeles Apparel 1807GD class), Ink body, ribbed cuffs. Longsleeve because the scene wears them to shows and the piece needs two arms.

Technique: 1-color plastisol, Cream, from hand-drawn art. The 801 marks are drawn once at full size by a letterer in chisel marker on a 13 x 17 in sheet, photocopied one generation and separated; the SVG jitter is a stand-in for that hand. Sleeve prints are a separate pass on a sleeve platen.

Placement and size: full back 13 x 17 in, 3 in below the collar seam; left chest X 3 x 3 in; wearer-left sleeve "801" 2.5 x 9 in reading down from the shoulder; wearer-right sleeve XXX 2.5 x 9 in.

Colorways: Ink body / Cream ink (main). Alt: Salt Pink pigment-dyed body / Ink ink (the pink flyer paper from R1, kept as a second run if the first sells).

Unit cost at a 50-unit test run: decorated-premium-blank lane, mid tier. Heavyweight longsleeve blank $9 to $12, three print locations with two setups on a 50 run roughly $9 to $12 per piece, woven label and hangtag under $1. Landed about $20 to $25, retails $60 to $70 DTC.

The one thing to verify before sampling: that the printer can hold a 13 x 17 in back on the chosen blank's body width in size S (some heavyweight longsleeves run narrow; the wall may need to drop to 12 x 16 in, which changes the row count, not the count).

What a local says: "Someone counted." Then they count a row to check.

Risk: 801 also covers Provo and Ogden; the shirt claims the whole Wasatch Front, not just the county. That is fine for a punk and may not be fine for a county DMO. If it matters, the count can run to 84101, the downtown ZIP, as 16,820 groups, which is a different and funnier object (a shirt that is solid cream from a distance) and would need a halftone separation instead of a hand drawing.

02 IT CAME FROM THE GREAT SALT LAKE (creature-feature tee, the hero)

File: 02-it-came-from-the-great-salt-lake-tee.svg

IN references: 05-brain-dead-sunn-o-tee.jpg (one grainy square on a plain body is enough), 31-flickr-flyer-c.jpg (xerox photo under heavy type, the inverse flyer bars), 30-flickr-flyer-b.jpg (cut-and-paste collage, one ink), 34-flickr-zine-a.jpg (zine black and white), 19-flickr-straight-edge.jpg (the X'd hands in the crowd), plus the brine shrimp entry in the symbol bank.

Idea: Artemia franciscana, the half-inch animal that is the lake's whole economy, blown up on a copier until it is a 1950s creature-feature monster rearing out of the pink north arm toward an all-ages crowd with its X'd hands up. Three scales on one shirt: the monster at fourteen inches, the crowd at an inch, and the same animal at life size on the upper back with "actual size" written beside it in marker, so the joke lands as you walk away.

What R2 pushed: the drawing. The shrimp now has a tapered abdomen of overlapping plates, a wide thorax, feathered phyllopods with setae reaching down for the crowd, stalked compound eyes with a halftone catchlight, mandibles, and the male's clasper antennae drawn as pincers. The sky is a stepped halftone (seven dot sizes, 22 degree screen) with copier streaks, the mountains are a flat ink silhouette with Antelope Island's humps, the water is a Salt Pink flood with ink wave lines and a splash where the tail breaks the surface, and the whole art has a rough-line displacement and 650 xerox specks. Title is a hand-lettered opener ("IT CAME FROM", slanted) over two lines of condensed poster type with a Salt Pink misregistration under both, like a two-color flyer printed a hair off. The crowd is two rows of silhouettes, front row with hair spikes, hands up, about half with a cream X knocked out of the back of the hand and the rest throwing two fingers.

Garment and fabric: 7 oz heavyweight boxy tee (Shaka Wear Max Heavyweight or LA Apparel 1801GD class), Cream, not optic white, so the print looks copied onto paper that has lived in a backpack.

Technique: 2-color screen print, water-based Ink and Salt Pink, pink down first, ink on top with a deliberate 1/16 in offset. Separations come off a real photocopy of the paste-up so every speck survives; the halftone sky is kept as a stochastic separation, not cleaned up. Back hit is one color, Ink.

Placement and size: front 14 x 15.5 in, 2 in below the collar seam; upper back 4 x 2 in, 1.5 in below the collar, shrimp printed at 0.5 in actual length.

Colorways: Cream body / Ink + Salt Pink (main). Alt: Ink body with the art flipped negative (Cream + Salt Pink inks), which turns the halftone sky into stars.

Unit cost at a 50-unit test run: decorated-premium-blank lane, mid tier. Heavyweight tee blank $7 to $10, two-color front plus one-color back on a 50 run roughly $8 to $11 per piece including three screens, label and tag under $1. Landed about $17 to $22, retails $50 to $60 DTC.

The one thing to verify before sampling: a press proof of the halftone sky at 110 mesh with water-based ink on the garment-dyed cream; if the small dots fill in, the sky moves to a coarser screen or to a hand-stippled version by the illustrator.

Finish by an illustrator: redraw the shrimp in brush and ink from this drawing at 2x, keep the segment count and the clasper pose, give the plates real overlap and the legs weight; hand-letter "IT CAME FROM" in a fat marker. Keep the crowd as cut-paper silhouettes, not drawn figures.

What a local says: "Sea-Monkey from hell." Then they explain to the visitor that the lake really is pink on the north side and that the shrimp are a $60-million-a-year harvest, which is the hangtag.

Risk: the title is a stock horror construction, not a scene phrase, and the CD accepted that in R1. The remaining risk is the Objects lane's scientific shrimp on the pouch; the two can share a round but should not share a table at the visitor center. Alternate flyer bars if VSL wants it closer to straight edge: "DRUG FREE" / "ALL AGES".

03 NOTHING TO DO IN SALT LAKE (three-phrase hoodie drop)

File: 03-nothing-to-do-in-salt-lake-hoodie.svg

IN references: 36-slc-punk-poster.jpg (white condensed title on black bars over a flat blue field), 26-slc-punk-still-b.jpg (the blue hair, the color trio), 08-pleasures-freak-tee-glitter.jpg (phrase-first single hit), 07-pleasures-suburbs-longsleeve-lookbook.jpg (heavy body, small wordmark logic).

Idea: A 14 oz hoodie with one sentence on it, split across the layout of the SLC Punk! poster: the first half in condensed cream type on a black title bar between two thin rules, then a flat blue flood left empty, with the second half of the sentence tucked along the flood's bottom edge. The empty blue is the nothing. R2 runs the drop as three approved phrases on three bodies, shown together: NOTHING TO DO / IN SALT LAKE on Ink, SALT LAKE IS / FOR THE WEIRD on Salt Pink, POSERS / GO TO PARK CITY on Cream. The hood is lined in the blue on all three so the trio shows with the hood down.

Garment and fabric: cross-grain 14 oz cotton fleece pullover hoodie (Los Angeles Apparel HF09 or House of Blanks class), hood lined in Poster Blue fleece, flat cream drawcords with metal tips (ink cords on the cream body).

Technique: 2-color plastisol, Cream and Poster Blue, the blue pulled as a flat flood with a dry-brush edge so it never reads as a corporate color block; on the Ink body the bar is the garment and only two colors print, on the Pink and Cream bodies the bar prints as a third color (Ink). The thin rules print in Cream on Ink and Pink bodies, in Ink on the Cream body.

Placement and size: front panel 11.5 x 13 in, top edge 3 in below the hood seam, bottom edge 1 in above the kangaroo pocket. No back print.

Colorways: Ink body (NOTHING TO DO IN SALT LAKE), Salt Pink body (SALT LAKE IS FOR THE WEIRD), Cream body (POSERS GO TO PARK CITY). Hood lining Poster Blue on all three. Phrases and bodies can be re-paired at the CD's call without any other change to the art.

Unit cost at a 50-unit test run: decorated-premium-blank lane, upper tier. 14 oz fleece blank $22 to $28, custom hood lining is a cut-and-sew step (an LA studio can line 50 hoods for roughly $6 to $9 each if the blank maker will ship unlined hoods, otherwise it waits for a 150-unit private-label run), two- or three-color front print on a 50 run roughly $7 to $10, label and tag about $1. Landed about $38 to $48 with the lining, $32 to $38 without, retails $120 to $140 DTC.

The one thing to verify before sampling: whether the blank maker will sell the hoodie with the hood lining omitted or in a specified color; if not, the blue hood lining becomes a blue hood interior print or drops, and the piece still works.

What a local says: "Yeah, that's what we said at 16, and then we went to Kilby every night." They buy POSERS GO TO PARK CITY for a friend who moved there.

Risk: POSERS GO TO PARK CITY names a neighboring destination; a county DMO printing it is the joke and also the thing legal will ask about. SALT LAKE IS FOR THE WEIRD is the safe lead if that phrase is held back. The SLC Punk! logotype is not reproduced anywhere; the piece uses the bar-and-flood structure and the palette only.

Performance

We run on Salt Lake

Lane thesis (unchanged): "We run on Salt Lake. Salt Lake is performance." Training alone more than race day, material shown close, the construction is the decoration.

What changed from R1

  • Every eyebrow is gone: no sheet header, no "FRONT / BACK" tracked caps, no spec strip, no coordinate line, no label-value block. The sheets are lookbook pages: garment large, one blown-up inset, swatches with plain names, a caption in sentences. Spec lives here.
  • 01 Shoreline (cut) is replaced by 01 Five A.M., a technical long sleeve where one of the approved hard-copy lines is the entire garment.
  • 02 Gain loses the elevation readout. The gain is now a graphic: one bonded strip running the full height of the body with 4,807 as the only type, read upward.
  • 03 Valley Floor keeps the single 4,219 but sets it like a race number on the cap (big, bib-spaced, satin stitch, brim crops it) and as a jacquard knit-in up the back of the sock calf.
  • Type: the condensed display face is shown as Oswald (Google) with Futura Extra Bold Condensed as the production face, which is what the 1990 Wieden+Kennedy inserts used. Sheet captions are Inter (Saans in production). Numerals on 02 and 03 are the same condensed face so the three pieces read as one system.
  • Palette: Mountain Navy, Cream, Rodeo Red, Sage, Ink, Sego Lily, with one Forest and one Sky second-run option. Reflective silver is a material, not a colour.

Fonts to load for the SVGs: Oswald 700, Inter 400/600, Source Serif 4 400 (Google Fonts). Fallbacks are declared in every text element.

01 Five A.M.

File: 01-five-am-bonded-longsleeve.svg (replaces 01 Shoreline; new slug, same slot)

IN references: 49-nike-1990-group-therapy-ad.jpg and 50-nike-1990-stress-management-ad.jpg (stacked condensed copy, talks straight to the runner), 48-wasatch-100-cody-priest-brighton-aid.jpg (headlamp, night, the work nobody sees), 32-bandit-coolgrid-singlet-flopack-detail.jpg (bonded hem, engineered mesh zones, one small mark), 07-district-vision-lab-tights-film.jpg (flat cold light for the shoot), 24-satisfy-mothtech-logo-detail.jpg (laser perforation kept, now only where it works: the gussets).

Idea: The approved line "Nobody is watching at 5 a.m. That is the point." is set stacked and huge across the chest of a bonded technical long sleeve, exactly like a 1990 W+K insert. It is printed in 3M Scotchlite reflective transfer, so by day it is a quiet grey on navy and in a headlamp or a car's lights it goes white. The garment literally says it only when nobody is watching.

Why this garment and fabric: A long sleeve is the dawn-patrol layer from October to April (tee under a vest is a summer thing). 118 gsm recycled polyester micro-eyelet jersey, bonded hem and cuffs, flatlock seams, laser-perforated underarm gussets (1.2 mm holes, 4 mm pitch, 2 x 3 in each) because the CO2 laser heat-seals polyester and this is the one place on a long sleeve that needs to dump heat under a pack strap.

Technique and why: 3M Scotchlite 8710 reflective heat-transfer film, one layer, no outline, no colour, centred chest, 9 x 11 in print area, five stacked lines in Futura Extra Bold Condensed caps, ragged-centred. Reflective film is the honest version of "performance": it is a safety material doing a design job. Second "SALT LAKE" Scotchlite hit at the back neck, 1.1 x 0.3 in. No front logo, no sleeve print. Salt-crystal icon on the woven size tab at the hem only.

Placement and size: chest block 9 in wide x 11 in tall, top of the block 2.5 in below the collar seam, centred on CF. Back neck 1.1 x 0.3 in, 1 in below the collar seam.

Colorways: Mountain Navy #13375D body, reflective grey by day / white when lit. Second run: Ink #212121 body; Forest #0D4C26 body. Reflective film does not change between colorways; the body does.

What a local would say: "That is the Shoreline at five in March." Then they will take a phone photo with the flash on to see it light up, which is the whole marketing plan.

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run: tier $$$$, roughly $38 to $55 landed using a stock technical long-sleeve blank (bonded-hem performance blank from a running-blank supplier) with the reflective transfer ($6 to $10 per placement at 50, film is expensive) and laser gussets done by a Utah laser shop. A true cut-and-sew version with our own pattern is not viable at 50 (research/merch/05, sampling dominates); it becomes viable at 250 through Portugal or a technical factory at $30 to $45. Retail $68 to $78 at the gear-adjacent tier.

One thing to verify before sampling: reflective film is stiff; an 11 in solid block of it can board the chest and crack at the fold. Sample at 50 percent halftone of the film (the lines still read white when lit, the hand stays soft) and compare to solid before committing.

Risk: A big grey block on navy is low contrast in daylight product photos. Shoot it twice, flat daylight and lit, and show both on the product page; the day shot alone undersells it.

02 Gain

File: 02-gain-alpha-pullover.svg

IN references: 21-polartec-alpha-direct-swatch.jpg (the loft is the garment), 36-nike-acg-lava-loft-official.jpg (one hard element on an honest soft garment), 43-blackdiamond-lcc-home-crag.jpg and 54-wasatch-avalanche-danger-kutv.jpg (the vertical is right there), 52-porcupine-hill-climb-2016-mccutcheon.jpg (the number on the climb), 03-arcteryx-system-a-drop6-fieldmag.jpg (run-to-the-climb layering).

Idea: A raglan quarter-zip in Polartec Alpha Direct 90 with one element on it: a bonded Pertex strip, 2.25 in wide, that runs from the hem to the collar seam beside the zip, and the number 4,807 set 1.6 in tall running up the strip. 4,807 is the gain from the downtown grid (4,219 ft) to the top of Mount Olympus (9,026 ft), the peak in every office window. The strip is the climb; you read the number the way you read it on the way up. No coordinates, no labels, nothing else.

Why this garment and fabric: Alpha Direct is the active-insulation fabric the Wasatch crowd knows by name; it breathes while you climb and needs no liner. A pullover keeps it a mid-layer under a shell on the skin track and over a tee on the Shoreline in March. 90 g/m² is the weight you can run uphill in.

Technique and why: Alpha Direct loft takes no ink and should not be needled, so the strip is the only place a print can live. Pertex Quantum Air 20D (35 gsm), Cream, bonded to the loft with a stitch-free edge, with a one-colour Ink heat transfer of the numerals. The strip is also a real construction detail: it is the one wind-blocking panel on the chest and gives the soft garment its only hard edge. YKK Vislon #3 quarter zip with cord pull, flatlock raglan seams, Lycra-bound hem and cuffs, 3M Scotchlite "SALT LAKE" at the back neck, salt-crystal icon on the woven size tab at the hem.

Placement and size: strip on the wearer's left front, 0.75 in from the zip tape, 2.25 in wide, full body length (about 26 in on a M), bonded. Numerals 1.6 in tall, rotated to read upward, baseline toward the zip, bottom of the numerals 1 in above the hem binding.

Colorways: Rodeo Red #A42F2C loft (Polartec Dawn lot, lab dip to match) with Cream #F6F1EC strip and Ink numerals. Second run: Mountain Navy #13375D loft with Sego Lily #FFDDA3 strip and Ink numerals.

What a local would say: "Olympus from Pete's Rock is 4,100, not 4,800." The number is from the grid, not the trailhead, because the point of this city is that you start downtown. That argument is the right argument to have, and it is the hang-tag copy.

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run: tier $$$$, roughly $75 to $110 landed. Polartec will not sell 50 units' worth of fabric direct (300 to 500 yard per-colour minimums); the route is a converter that stocks Alpha Direct by the yard (Discovery Fabrics type, about 1.5 yd per unit at retail yardage) plus Pertex offcuts, sewn by a small domestic technical shop with a pattern we own, with the $500 to $1,500 development amortised over 50. At 250 units through a Wasatch brand that already holds the Polartec relationship (Black Diamond, Kuhl) this drops to $45 to $65. Retail $160 to $180, gear tier.

One thing to verify before sampling: that the bonding adhesive holds a 26 in Pertex strip to an open-grid loft through 20 washes without the loft pulling through or the strip puckering at the hem binding. Sample a 6 in strip first, wash-test, then cut the full one.

Risk: Alpha Direct snags and sheds; the strip edge is a snag line. Keep the bond edge inside the strip (no raw Pertex edge) and say "it sheds a little" on the product page, the way Norrøna does.

03 Valley Floor

File: 03-valley-floor-cap-sock.svg

IN references: 34-ciele-fstcap-elite.jpg (perforated panels, reflective trim, no hardware), 41-tracksmith-us-trials-emily-maye.jpg (the number pinned to the body), 44-speedgoat-50k-2024-sinclair-irunfar.jpg (bib on the ridge), 40-tracksmith-amateur-spirit-cover.jpg (the kit you wear every day), 35-norda-blackdiamond-fkt-poles.jpg (one mark, all function), 52-porcupine-hill-climb-2016-mccutcheon.jpg (every climb starts on the valley floor).

Idea: A perforated five-panel running cap and a merino crew sock carrying one number, 4,219, the valley-floor elevation on the airport sign. On the cap it is set like a race bib: big, bib-spaced numerals in satin stitch, low on the side panel so the brim edge crops the baseline. On the sock it is a jacquard knit-in running up the back of the calf, facing whoever is behind you.

Why this garment and fabric: Hats are most of what a visitor buys and Ciele built a brand on one cap. 85 gsm four-way stretch recycled ripstop so it packs into a vest pocket; laser-perforated side and back panels (1.2 mm, 4 mm pitch) for the same reason the FSTCap has them. Sock: 58 percent 18.5-micron merino, 39 nylon, 3 elastane, 200-needle, because merino is the mountain-town fibre and a knit-in numeral is a knit decision, not a print.

Technique and why: Cap: satin-stitch embroidery, 1.6 in numerals, Ink on Cream, wearer's left side panel, about 7,000 stitches, over a tear-away stabiliser because the panel is perforated. 3M Scotchlite bound brim edge as the only reflective; Coolmax sweatband; elastic back, no buckle, no eyelets. Sock: jacquard knit-in numerals 1.75 in tall up the back of the calf, Cream on Mountain Navy, single 0.4 in Sage arch band, Y-heel gore, hand-linked toe. Salt-crystal icon on the woven sweatband label only. Sold as a set in a printed glassine sleeve.

Placement and size: cap numerals 1.6 in tall, bib letterspacing, centred on the left side panel, baseline 0.25 in above the brim seam so the brim visually crops it. Sock numerals 1.75 in tall, centre back, starting 0.75 in above the heel gore and reading upward.

Colorways: Cream #F6F1EC cap with Ink #212121 numerals; Mountain Navy #13375D sock with Cream numerals and Sage #8DCEA8 arch band. Second run: Sky #147CB2 cap with Cream numerals; Cream sock with Navy numerals.

What a local would say: "It's the elevation on the airport sign." Then: "Where's the front logo?" There isn't one. That absence is the status signal for the person who skis 20 days a year on a lunch break.

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run: tier $$ for the set, roughly $28 to $40 landed. Cap: an embroidered blank cap at 50 is $14 to $18 (research/merch/05), plus $4 to $8 to step up to a stock laser-perforated ripstop running blank, so $18 to $26. A fully custom cap is 150-plus overseas; not at 50. Sock: a domestic small-batch sock mill with a 50-pair minimum runs $9 to $14 a pair for a two-colour jacquard with a one-time $75 to $150 pattern set-up. Retail $64 for the set ($44 cap, $24 sock sold separately later), accessible tier.

One thing to verify before sampling: that satin stitch at 1.6 in over perforated ripstop does not pucker or tear out at the hole line; sample with tear-away and with a cut-away stabiliser and pick the one that lies flat after a wet-dry cycle. On the sock, confirm the mill can knit a 1.75 in numeral without the float on the reverse snagging a toenail (ask for a floats-tied sample).

Risk: A number alone can read as arbitrary to a visitor; the sleeve carries the one line "4,219 ft. The valley floor. Everything here is uphill from it." and the deck shows the cap next to the Gain fleece so the two numbers read as one system.

Objects

The unseen objects of a Salt Lake day

What changed from R1: the eyebrows are gone. That means the sheet header, the tracked-caps captions, the coordinate and elevation strings, the spec strip, and the Le Labo fill-in label on the case (cut) and on the LP back ("Recorded by: ____"). Each sheet is now a lookbook page. The object is large, one detail is blown up in an inset, colorways are named swatches, and the captions are plain sentences. The spec lives here. Two pieces were approved (02 LP, 03 Artemia). The 01 goggle case was cut and is replaced by the CD's own example: a rack for skis or a board.

The fonts in the SVGs are stand-ins. Ivar Display and Saans are named first, with Georgia and Inter as fallbacks; swap to the licensed families for production. Hand-drawn character comes from SVG turbulence filters: rough on the jetty and the label spiral, grain on the sleeve and the leather. These filters drop out in some renderers, so judge the sheets in a browser.

Cost tiers are per finished unit at a 50-unit test run, using the $ scale from research/merch/05 (under $2 / $2–5 / $5–10 / over $10). All three objects land in $$$$ because none is a decorated blank. Each line gives a working estimate, marked (est.), to replace with a written quote. Section 05 has no hardgoods price table, so these are trade rule-of-thumb figures, not cited ones.

01. Two Arms (replaces the goggle case)

File: 01-two-arms-rack.svg

IN references: 45-storeyourboard-vail-wood-ski-rack (a single oak bar on the wall, the gear hung as the display: the direct source), 50-brine-shrimp-dwr (the shrimp, the lane's one mascot), 06-parksproject-brass-french-press (an honest material object for daily use), 23-loewe-craft-prize-2025-winner-aoki (credit the maker: a Salt Lake woodshop).

Idea: A 30-inch solid white oak rail with two felt-topped arms. It holds one snowboard laid across, or one pair of skis standing tails-down, bases to the wall. The only decoration is the brine shrimp burned into the right end of the rail with the same brass die that debosses the Artemia pouch, so the two objects read as one family.

Why this object and material: Everyone here who rides has a board leaning in a hallway. The rack is the thing you screw into the wall of your first apartment after your first season, and it shows where you live without saying so. White oak is hard, stable, and takes a brand cleanly. The arms tilt 6 degrees with a lip at the end so nothing rolls off, and the wool felt protects topsheets and edges.

Spec

  • Maker: a Salt Lake furniture or woodshop (CNC plus hand finish). The alternative is a powder-coat fabricator for the steel version.
  • Material: rail in white oak, 30 × 3.5 × 1.25 in. Two arms, 6 × 1.5 × 1.5 in, mortised and glued into the rail, tilted 6°, with a 1 in lip. Hardwax oil finish (Rubio or Osmo).
  • Pads: 3 mm wool felt in Forest, glued to the top of each arm.
  • Decoration: brand burned in at 2.75 in wide, right end of the rail, centered on its height. Heated brass die shared with the pouch, so it is one tooling cost for two products.
  • Mounting: two 5/16 lag bolts into studs at 16 in centers, under oak plugs. Hardware and a paper template come in the box.
  • Colorways: White Oak / Forest felt (hero). Mountain Navy powder-coated 3/16 steel, with the shrimp laser-etched through the coat to bare metal. Sego Lily: soaped ash, the lightest and cheapest option.
  • Packaging: kraft box with a printed sleeve. No fill-in label.
  • Cost tier at 50 units: $$$$. Oak version about $45–75 a unit (est.) at a local shop, plus a one-time brass die of $150–300 (est.) that the pouch shares. Steel version about $35–55 a unit (est.), with a one-time $150–400 for the laser file and fixture (est.). Retail target $145–185 for oak.
  • Verify before sampling: that the burned shrimp holds its eleven pairs of legs at 2.75 in on oak end-adjacent grain. If the legs fill in, enlarge the brand to 3.5 in or simplify the hatching for the wood die only.

What a local would say: "That's a sea monkey on my ski rack." Then they explain it to every guest.

Risk: A rack is a big, heavy SKU for a visitor center. It needs to sell online and at a few shops with local shipping, not from the airport. The 157 cm board shown takes almost the full width of a studio wall, so the sheet shows real scale on purpose.

02. Field Recordings, Great Salt Lake

File: 02-field-recordings-lp.svg

IN references: 54-a24-primetime-vinyl (the sleeve as a real cover, the disc sliding out), 31-spiral-jetty-uibel-aerial (the cover illustration: playa, bank and dirt road, black basalt arm, spiral, pink water), 21-nasa-iss-great-salt-lake (the split pour), 32-great-salt-lake-salt-crystals-imaggeo (the crust pattern and the small hopper-crystal mark on the back), 23-loewe-craft-prize-2025-winner-aoki (the recordist named on every pressing).

What R2 pushed:

  • The front is now an illustrated aerial of the jetty in the pink north arm, with the title set in Ivar like a record cover, not a spec. The recordist is credited on the front.
  • The back is set like an LP back: a title, then large serif A and B side letters, numbered tracks with times, and a short credit block. There is no data table and no fill-in line.
  • The label carries the jetty spiral, counter-clockwise as built, and is shown at full size in the inset.
  • The disc is a split pour, pink over blue, with a soft irregular seam at the causeway angle.

Recordist slot: the sheet shows "[Recordist]" as a named placeholder, not a blank. Candidate approach: commission one Utah field recordist or sound artist (for example, from the U of U or Westminster sound-art programs, or a local ambient label) and give them the front credit. Their name prints. Nobody fills it in by hand.

Spec

  • Pressing: a 12 in LP, 180 g, 33 1/3, from a US plant that does split color (Furnace MFG, Precision, or Hand Drawn Pressing).
  • Disc: split pour, Salt Pink over Sky. Ask the plant for its closest match to PMS 2339 C / 2390 C.
  • Label: 100 mm uncoated, one color Ink. Side B is the same spiral at 60%.
  • Jacket: 3 mm spine, reverse-board 24 pt, four-color litho (illustrated front) with a matte finish. A poly-lined inner. A 4 × 6 postcard download card.
  • Placement: title lower left on the front, recordist lower right, catalog number top right. The credits block is on the back.
  • Colorways: one pressing. The pour varies by nature, which is the point.
  • Cost tier at 50 units: $$$$. Vinyl does not run at 50 economically. Plants quote 100 minimum and are cheapest at 300. At 100 units, a split-color 180 g run with a printed jacket lands around $14–22 a unit plus about $800–1,200 in lacquers, plates and test pressings (est.), which is $25–35 a unit all-in at 100 (est.). At 50 the per-unit figure roughly doubles. The honest test is 100 with 50 held back for gifting and press. Recording and mastering fees are extra. Retail target $40–48.
  • Verify before sampling: written permission from the Holt/Smithson Foundation for the jetty image on the sleeve and label. Also location-recording releases from Alta (A2) and UTA (A5). If the Foundation declines, the cover becomes the salt-crust and pink-water field without the jetty, the label becomes the hopper crystal, and the piece still stands.

What a local would say: "A2 is the Wildcat lift. I'd know that hum anywhere."

Risk: The rights described above, and lead time. Plants run 10–16 weeks, so the record has to be booked for the season it describes.

03. Artemia

File: 03-artemia-pouch.svg

IN references: 36-ald-leather-keychain-pouch (a small carried leather piece with brass hardware and one quiet mark), 50-brine-shrimp-dwr (the drawing's source: female, stalked eyes, eleven pairs of leaf legs, brood sac, forked tail), 06-parksproject-brass-french-press (brass, honest materials), 23-loewe-craft-prize-2025-winner-aoki (the maker's name stamped inside).

What R2 pushed:

  • The die art is now a natural-history plate: stalked eyes, antennae, segmented thorax, eleven phyllopodia with gill lobes, veins and setae, far-side legs in a lighter weight for depth, a brood sac with eggs, a segmented abdomen, and a furca with setae.
  • The pouch is shown in a hand at scale (1 in = 60 px), so its size reads instantly.
  • The back shows the exterior card slot with a transit card in it.
  • The R1 caption strip is gone.

Spec

  • Maker: a Salt Lake leatherworker, credited by name in the inside stamp ("[Leatherworker]" is a placeholder for the real name, not a blank).
  • Material: 3.5 oz full-grain veg-tan. Natural (Sego Lily, darkening to honey) is the hero; black veg-tan is the Ink colorway. Unlined, with painted edges.
  • Size: 4.5 × 3 in. A #3 brass zip along the top. A brass swivel hook on a leather tab. An exterior card slot on the back.
  • Decoration: blind deboss with a brass die, 2.75 in wide, centered on the front, about 0.4 mm deep. No foil and no ink. Inside, a 6 pt blind stamp reads "Full grain. Made in Utah. Carry it daily." with the maker's name.
  • Colorways: Natural, Honey (the same hide at a year, shown for the story, not a separate SKU), Ink.
  • Cost tier at 50 units: $$$$. About $28–45 a unit (est.) from a local maker: leather, YKK brass zip, solid brass hook, and labor. Add a one-time $150–300 for the brass die (est.), shared with the rack. Retail target $85–110.
  • Verify before sampling: that the die holds the leg hatching at 2.75 in. Strike one test on scrap veg-tan. If the hatching closes up, the illustrator thins it for the leather die while the plate keeps full detail for print and the rack brand.

What a local would say: "Is that a brine shrimp? Sea monkeys. That's the state crustacean, right?"

Risk: The drawing. The SVG sets the anatomy and composition; a natural-history illustrator still has to redraw it by hand before the die is cut, or it reads as a bug instead of a crest.

Neo-Western

Rancher at 7,000 feet

All three R1 pieces were marked IN, so there is no replacement slot. Round 2 pushes the drawing on each one and resolves the two R1 flags. Lane thesis stays "Rancher at 7,000 feet": quiet workwear, real craft, the place named plainly.

What changed everywhere

  • Sheets are lookbook pages now: a name, one italic line, the garment large, the detail blown up, colorways as named swatches, a caption in sentences. No sheet header, no spec strip, no tracked-caps labels, no coordinates or elevations anywhere. The spec lives here.
  • The hidden cuff stitch on 01 is no longer "Albion Basin, 9,500 ft". It is the place name alone, in script: "Albion Basin". The script in the file is Pinyon Script as a placeholder; a letterer draws the real one.
  • The bison patch on 02 carries 1893, the year bison were put on Antelope Island (symbol bank, verified). It is the herd date, not the roundup date, and the sheet says so in plain words under the patch. The roundup's founding year is unsettled in our files (1987 vs 1989), so we do not print it.
  • The rag on 03 no longer says "Days of '47" anywhere. The headline is "Pioneer Day", the public holiday, and the image carries the event. No license needed. The reference flag from R1 stands: 19-days-of-47-longhorn-drive-slc.jpg in the moodboard folder is a meetinghouse photo, not the drive; the illustrator works from the Church News gallery URL in captions.md.
  • Type: Ivar is still the intent for titles and the rag headline (Playfair Display stands in). Inter stands in for Saans on swatch names and the small sentences. Nothing is set in tracked caps.
  • Palette by hex from BRAND-DIGEST.md only. No off-palette hit in this lane. Veg-tan leather and brass are materials, not colors.

Fonts named in the SVGs: Playfair Display, Inter, Pinyon Script (Google Fonts), with Georgia / Helvetica / cursive fallbacks.

01 Paintbrush Yoke Shirt

File: 01-paintbrush-yoke-shirt.svg

What is on the sheet: the shirt from the back with the yoke embroidery in place; the embroidery at thread scale in an inset; the left cuff turned back to show the script; two colorways with their thread sets; the plain front, small.

The drawing, R2: the botanical is now built as chain stitch, not as line art. Every stroke is a row of linked loops that follows the direction a 114w103 would run it: bracts of the paintbrush are three parallel rows from base to tip with the split tips as two short diverging rows, the lower bracts go to Sage the way the real plant does at the base; the lupine florets are small looped rings stacked in pairs up the spike, Sky low and Light Sky high, with a Cream keel stitch in the top florets; the lupine leaf is seven leaflets radiating from one point; stems are two rows side by side (Sage and Meadow) so they read as a stalk, not a wire; grass and a loose ground row in Sage. Three paintbrush stalks at three heights, two lupine spikes, a fifth paintbrush low and small. What a chain-stitch artisan finishes: the real loop count (the file is a stand-in at about 6 px per loop), the fill density in the bract heads, and the thread shading between Rodeo Red and Terracotta.

Blank or maker: a plain western snap shirt in 7 oz brushed cotton twill, pointed back yoke, pearl snaps with copper rims, cuff facing in self fabric. Sourcing route for the 50-unit test: a stock blank western shirt from a workwear maker, re-labeled, rather than cut-and-sew (see cost). Summer alt: 5.5 oz chambray.

Technique: hand-guided chain stitch (Singer 114w103 or Cornely) for the hero run; six thread colors (Rodeo Red, Terracotta, Sky, Light Sky, Sage, Meadow). Cuff script in Sego Lily chain stitch, 5 x 0.7 in, on the inside cuff facing of the left sleeve so it shows only when rolled.

Placement and size: yoke motif 4.5 x 3.5 in, centered on the back, top of the tallest bract 1.25 in below the collar seam. Front is empty. Neck label: woven, "Salt Lake" in Ivar italic, the small salt-crystal line icon beside it; no VSL logo.

Colorways: Mountain Navy twill (paintbrush Rodeo Red and Terracotta, lupine Sky and Light Sky, Sage and Meadow stems, Sego Lily cuff script). Rodeo Red twill (paintbrush Sego Lily and Aspen Gold, lupine Sky and Cream, same stems, Cream cuff script).

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run (est., from research/merch/05): a plain blank western snap shirt sourced from a workwear maker runs $28 to $45 wholesale; machine chain stitch (Cornely multi-head) at this size is $8 to $15 per placement at 50 pieces, two placements; labels and relabel $1 to $2; landed roughly $48 to $75 per unit, which is the $$$$ decoration tier. Hand-guided artisan chain stitch (Fort Lonesome type) is $25 to $150 per piece and makes this a numbered launch piece at $150 to $350 retail, which is the brand's chain-stitch price band. Custom cut-and-sew is not viable at 50 (development $500 to $1,500 before the first shirt).

One thing to verify before sampling: that a domestic multi-head chain-stitch house can hold six thread changes in a 4.5 in motif at 50 pieces without the loops closing up; ask for a sew-out on the actual twill, not on a swatch of broadcloth.

What a local would say: "That's paintbrush. You've been up Little Cottonwood in July." Then they roll the cuff.

Risk: chain stitch at any scale means a specialist shop and a lead time measured in months. If the test run has to be fast, run a flat-embroidery version of the same drawing and keep the chain stitch for the hero 24.

02 Island Herd Chore Coat

File: 02-island-herd-chore-coat.svg

What is on the sheet: the coat opened flat so the whole lining shows, fronts folded out; the leather patch at hand scale in an inset with a plain sentence under it giving the date's meaning; the coat closed, small, with the patch on the chest pocket; two shell colorways; one quilt block at repeat size with a sentence on how it is made.

The drawing, R2: the garment is shown open, as asked. The lining is a half-square-triangle quilt built in pinwheel blocks, one block three inches, in Cream, Sego Lily, Aspen Gold, Terracotta and Rodeo Red, with the piecing seams drawn as thin lines and the channel quilting as a dashed diagonal, one direction, the way it will actually be stitched. The bison on the patch is a proper silhouette now (hump, low head, beard, horns, four legs) instead of massing. The patch reads "Antelope Island" in Ivar italic along the top, the bison across the middle, and "1893" large in Ivar bold at the bottom left: the year is the graphic, not a caption. A leather grain filter sits on the patch in the file; the hot-stamp die is cut from the vector.

Blank or maker: cut-and-sew, domestic (LA or Texas studio) for the hero; for the 50-unit test, a stock waxed-canvas chore coat blank from a workwear maker, re-lined. 10 oz waxed cotton canvas shell, Ink corduroy collar, corozo buttons, two hip pockets and one chest pocket, hanging loop.

Technique: lining is printed cotton sateen (the quilt is a print, not pieced) channel-quilted on the diagonal over 4 oz fill. Patch is veg-tan leather, 2 x 1.25 in, hot-stamp debossed, no ink, sewn to the chest pocket on all four sides. Neck label as on 01.

Placement and size: patch centered on the chest pocket, 0.5 in below the pocket's top edge. Lining covers body and sleeves. No other marks outside.

Colorways: Forest waxed canvas with the Cream, Sego Lily, Aspen Gold, Terracotta, Rodeo Red quilt. Mountain Navy waxed canvas with the same quilt (navy is the lake on the drive out to the island).

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run (est., from research/merch/05): a fully custom waxed-canvas coat with printed quilted lining is lane-two cut-and-sew at the very bottom of its MOQ; landed $120 to $180 per unit plus $1,500 to $3,000 of development (pattern, two samples, lining print strike-off), and waxed canvas from a UK or Pacific Northwest mill carries a yardage minimum that 50 coats may not reach. That is a $320 to $380 retail garment and not a test-run product. The honest 50-unit test is the patch and the lining print on a stock waxed chore coat blank ($55 to $85 wholesale), re-lined by a local sewing shop at $25 to $40 per coat, patch $2 to $4 each at 50, landed roughly $85 to $130, which is the $$$$ tier. Price it as a hero at $240 to $280 and treat the first run as the sample order.

One thing to verify before sampling: the lining print on sateen. Print one yard, quilt it, and look at it under shop light; if it reads as a motel bedspread the whole piece fails. Also confirm the leather patch supplier can deboss a 58 pt numeral cleanly at 2 in.

What a local would say: "Roundup coat." Then they open it.

Risk: weight, warmth and price limit the selling window to October through March, and a re-lined blank has a label that is not ours unless the maker allows relabeling; confirm before ordering blanks.

03 Main Street Drive Wild Rag

File: 03-main-street-drive-wild-rag.svg

What is on the sheet: the rag flat at 22 x 22 in with the finished one-color drawing; the rag tied at the throat over a Forest chore coat collar, with the skyline in the fold and the herd in the tails; the brass bolo slide with the same steer; three colorways with small flats of the second and third.

The drawing, R2: one picture in one color. Two Wasatch ridgelines with hatched slopes, a downtown massing of thirteen towers with windows knocked out of the ink and hatched shadow sides, the street with the rails as two long lines and ties, the curb below, three ranks of longhorns walking right (ten in the far rank, eight, then six near), three riders (one on point ahead of the near rank, one at the back, one in the middle distance), dust and hoof marks on the street. Headline "Pioneer Day" in Ivar bold with a rule under it, corner horn marks, double-rule hem, the statement in Ivar italic: "Longhorns down Main Street, the mountains behind the towers. Every July." and "Salt Lake" at the foot. A turbulence displacement filter roughens the ink for the sheet; the illustrator redraws the steers and riders as dry-brush line from the Church News photo and keeps the layout. Skyline stays generic massing: no temple, no branded tower.

Blank or maker: 22 x 22 in 12 mm silk twill with hand-rolled hem for the hero; 4.5 oz cotton voile with a machine-rolled hem for the core price. Bolo slide: engraved brass, 1.5 in, white enamel field, braided leather cord with brass tips.

Technique: one-color water-based screen print, 20 x 20 in image area, one screen. Printed before hemming. Bolo slide engraved from the same vector steer.

Placement and size: print centered on the square; headline cap height 2.5 in; herd band 4 in tall across the full width; the rag folds on the diagonal into a 2 in band so the skyline lands in the knot and the herd in the tails (shown on the sheet).

Colorways: Mountain Navy on Sego Lily (lead), Rodeo Red on Cream (second drop), Sage on Forest (third drop; printed in Sage on a Forest-dyed blank).

Estimated unit cost at a 50-unit test run (est., from research/merch/05): a blank 22 in silk twill square with hand-rolled hem from a scarf maker is $9 to $16 at 50; one-color water-based screen print $3 to $6 per piece at this quantity with $40 to $60 of screen setup amortized; label $0.50; landed silk roughly $14 to $24 per unit ($ to $$ decoration tier). Cotton voile blank $2.50 to $4.50, landed $7 to $12. Bolo slide, engraved brass with enamel at an MOQ of 50 to 100: $7 to $14 each, sold as a set with the silk at $85 to $95 or alone at $28. The rag is the lane's volume product and the only one that clears the brand's margin ladder at 50 units.

One thing to verify before sampling: water-based ink on silk twill. Some shops will only print silk with discharge or pigment; ask for a strike-off on the actual silk and wash it twice before approving the hand.

What a local would say: "That's the cattle drive. They shut down Main for it."

Risk: the illustrator's redraw has to stay one color and keep the knockout windows legible at 20 in; if the drawing gets busier than this file it stops folding well. Hold the line count.

Latino

Latin life in the West

All three R1 pieces were marked IN. R2 pushes each toward a finished thing: the jersey is a full kit, Vecino is a drawn script rather than a font, and the lotería cards are illustrated cards shown as the back print and as a card set. The sheets are lookbook pages now: garment large, detail blown up, colorways as named swatches, a plain caption. No header line, no spec strip, no label-value blocks. The spec lives here.

Who designs this (unchanged, and still the point). These are a starting brief, not finished artwork. The line is designed by Latino designers from Salt Lake County (West Valley, Rose Park, Glendale first), with a letterer and an illustrator from the community redrawing everything in these files, and a revenue share written into the deal with a community org (Centro Civico Mexicano or Comunidades Unidas; the Kids of Immigrants x CHIRLA model, org on the hangtag, money going back). VSL is licensor and curator, not author. The test for every piece: would the community wear it to a Sunday car show.

Shared label on all three: interior neck label with the small salt-crystal line icon, "Diseñado en Salt Lake County," and the partner-org line. No VSL logo in the artwork. The eight-place hem list from R1 moved off the outside of the jersey (it read as a caption); it is now printed inside the back neck, under the label.

Fonts in the SVGs are stand-ins named by Google font (Pirata One, Anton, Playfair Display, Archivo Narrow). Vecino is no longer a font: the word is drawn as stroked paths so the weight can vary. The sheet background is Cream, not white, so the files sit together as pages.

Cost tiers below use research/merch/05-production-logistics-and-audience.md: lane one (decorated premium blank) lands at roughly $9 to $30 per finished unit at 24 to 72 piece minimums; lane two (cut-and-sew) at $25 to $90+ with MOQs of 50 to 300. A 50-unit test run sits at the expensive end of every range because screens, digitizing and pattern work amortize over 50 pieces, not 500.

01 · Club Deportivo Salt Lake jersey

File: 01-club-deportivo-salt-lake-jersey.svg

IN references: 09-paisaboys-club-deportivo-tee.jpg, 10-paisaboys-doce-estrellas-jacket.jpg, 03-bxr-worldwide-mexico.jpg, 07-koi-nike-jersey.jpg, 35-sltrib-la-barra-real-2021.jpg, 42-ksl-latino-world-cup-utah-2026.jpg.

What changed in R2. It is a kit now, not a diagram. Front: v-neck collar and cuffs in Forest with a Cream keyline, Forest side panels, bird's-eye mesh drawn as texture, crest on the wearer's left chest, 801 block on the right, four twill stars down each sleeve. Back: SALT LAKE arched in blackletter with a Cream keyline over 801 in two-color tackle twill at full number height. The crest is blown up as the embroidered badge it will be: merrowed Cream edge, satin-stitch direction on the Forest field and the ridge, the brine shrimp redrawn segmented with a fringe of legs, stalked eyes, antennae and a forked tail, the lake as a Salt Pink band under the ridge. The sleeve star is shown at size as Forest twill with a Cream running stitch. The match-day alt is drawn small: Rodeo Red body, Mountain Navy trim, same crest, Cream number.

Blank or maker. Cut-and-sew, Los Angeles (Bomme, Lefty or Indie Source tier), from a tech pack. There is no stock blank that gives a drop-shoulder v-neck mesh jersey in Salt Pink with Forest panels; the sublimated retail tier can use a stock sublimation jersey blank if the budget forces it, but the colors then come from the printer, not the dye house.

Fabric. 160 gsm recycled polyester bird's-eye mesh body, 220 gsm flat-knit polyester rib for collar and cuffs in Forest, Cream keyline knitted in. Sized up and boxy, worn loose over a tee.

Technique. Crest: 3.5 in diameter embroidered patch, roughly 18,000 stitches, merrowed edge, sewn on (not heat-sealed) so it can also be sold alone at $14 to $18 retail. Stars: 1 in tackle twill appliqué, Forest twill with a Cream running stitch, four per sleeve. Back name and number: 2-color tackle twill (Forest on Cream), SALT LAKE at 1.75 in cap height on a 10 in arc, 801 at 10 in number height. Retail tier: the same art sublimated, crest still a sewn patch.

Placement and size. Crest centered 3 in below the collar point on the wearer's left, 801 block 1.5 in cap height mirrored on the right. Stars from 1.5 in below the shoulder seam, 1.4 in apart on center, following the sleeve edge. Back arch top at 2.5 in below the collar; number baseline 4 in above hem. Eight place names printed inside the back neck, 0.25 in cap height, plain.

Colorways. Home: Salt Pink #F58B88 body, Forest #0D4C26 trim, panels and twill, Cream #F6F1EC keyline. Match-day alt: Rodeo Red #A42F2C body, Mountain Navy #13375D trim, Cream keyline and number, only with La Barra Real co-signing.

Estimated unit cost, 50-unit test run. Lane two. Cut-and-sew mesh jersey with custom rib at 50 pieces: $28 to $38 per unit for the garment, plus $9 to $12 for the patch, twill stars and twill number at that quantity, plus $4 to $6 in pattern, grading and sample fees amortized over 50. Call it $45 to $60 landed. Retail $110 to $130 at DTC multiples. The sublimated tier lands at $26 to $34 and retails $70 to $85.

One thing to verify before sampling. Clearance on 801 as a mark in apparel (Utah USPTO and state searches), and a sit-down with La Barra Real before the first sample, because the alt colorway lives or dies on their blessing.

Who finishes it. A Salt Lake County embroidery digitizer draws the crest for thread (the SVG is the layout, not the stitch file). A community letterer redraws SALT LAKE in a blackletter that is theirs, not Pirata One. The eight-place list and count stay with the community designers; the Salt Lake City-only six-star version is the fallback.

What a local would say. "Which club is that?" "Nosotros."

Risk. Same as R1 and still real: a supporters' kit for a club that does not exist can read as a knockoff to RSL and the barra. The upside of that risk is a co-signed version for the barra, which is why they are in the room before sample one.

02 · Vecino

File: 02-vecino-fine-line-tee.svg

IN references: 01-bxr-hyna-tee.jpg, 25-mister-cartoon-by-oriol-1994.jpg, 05-koi-this-is-for-our-family-tee.jpg, 13-estevan-oriol-lamag.jpg, 26-cdmx-rotulos-zocalo.jpg.

What changed in R2. The word is drawn, not typeset. Vecino is a set of stroked paths in one continuous line: hairline on the up strokes, pressure on the down strokes (the V stem, the i, the n stems, the bowl of the o), an entry flourish on the V, a dotted i, and the tail of the o swinging up and over, then back under the whole word as the underline, thinning to nothing at the left. A light displacement filter roughs the edge the way a liner on cotton does. VECINA is on the sheet on the women's cut: same drawing, the o replaced by an a with a heavy stem, same tail. 801 at the back neck is drawn in the same line. The lettering is shown at print size, thirteen inches, on a black field.

Blank or maker. Los Angeles Apparel 1801GD (6.5 oz, garment-dyed, made in Los Angeles) for the hero tier; Shaka Wear SHMHSS Max Heavyweight (7.5 oz) if the drop needs to come in cheaper. The women's cut is the same blank in a cropped boxy fit, not a slim "ladies" tee.

Fabric. 6.5 to 7.5 oz ringspun cotton, garment-dyed Ink and enzyme-washed so the surface is soft enough for a hairline. The BxR tee is black with white ink because the line needs the contrast.

Technique. One-color water-based white screen print, 230 mesh, one pass, no underbase. The letterer draws the final in ink on vellum, scanned at 1200 dpi, vectorized without smoothing so the hand stays. Strike-off on the actual blank, approved by the letterer, before the run. If the line fills, go up a mesh, not down a line weight.

Placement and size. Front, 13 x 5 in, centered, top of the V flourish 3 in below the collar seam. Back neck, 801 at 1.25 in wide, 1 in below the collar. Hem: nothing on the outside. "Diseñado en Salt Lake County" and the partner line are on the interior label only.

Colorways. Ink #212121 body, white ink. Second run: Forest #0D4C26 body, Cream #F6F1EC ink. Vecina: Mountain Navy #13375D body, Salt Pink #F58B88 ink.

Estimated unit cost, 50-unit test run. Lane one. LAA 1801GD at $9 to $12 plus a one-color print at 50 pieces ($4 to $6 with the screen amortized) plus a woven label and relabel ($1.50 to $2): $15 to $20 landed. On Shaka, $10 to $14. Retail $48 to $55. This is the cheapest piece in the lane to test and should go first.

One thing to verify before sampling. That the letterer's thinnest stroke survives at 230 mesh on garment-dyed cotton: print the hairline test strip (0.5, 0.75, 1.0 pt) on the actual blank before the word is finalized, and let the result set the minimum weight in the drawing.

Who finishes it. A Salt Lake County letterer with a fine-line hand. The paths in the SVG set the composition (flourish height, tail length, where the weight sits); the letterer owns every curve.

What a local would say. "That's it? Yeah, that's it."

Risk. Fine-line script is unforgiving in production; a filled-in line looks cheap on a $50 shirt. The strike-off and the letterer in the approval chain are the whole mitigation.

03 · Lotería Salt Lake

File: 03-loteria-salt-lake-tee.svg

IN references: 47-loteria-boards.jpg, 26-cdmx-rotulos-zocalo.jpg, 15-ksl-hispanic-heritage-utah.jpg, 19-sltrib-lowrider-urban-arts-2019.jpg, 20-ksl-utah-lowrider-community.jpg, 41-deseret-jaripeo-days-of-47-2019.jpg.

What changed in R2. The six cards are illustrated cards now, 2:3 in Don Clemente proportions, with a big serif numeral on a plate top left and the name in a lotería serif on the foot rule. Each image is a scene with line art, flat spot fills, hatching for shade, and the fills deliberately pushed 1 to 2 px off the line so the registration is imperfect, the way the real cards are. El Trax is a red TRAX car under its pantograph with the Wasatch behind. La Montaña is the ridge with snow on the peaks, a sun, foothills and the valley floor. El Taco is three al pastor on a plate under the trompo, with lime and radish. La Sal is a halite cluster on a crust with the pink north arm behind it. El Camarón is the brine shrimp drawn like the DWR drawing: segmented body, eleven pairs of leaf-shaped legs, stalked eyes, antennae, forked tail. La Troca is a single cab laid low on chrome wires under a Terracotta ridge. The sheet shows the board on the back of the tee, El Camarón on the chest, the cards as a fanned set, and three of them at size with card-stock grain.

Blank or maker. Los Angeles Apparel 1801GD in Ink, XS to 4XL, because car-club sizing runs big. Shaka SHMHSS as the cheaper fallback. Card set: a Salt Lake offset printer on 14 pt uncoated stock, boxed, with a printed game sheet.

Fabric. 6.5 oz ringspun cotton, garment-dyed Ink. Black makes the card palette pop the way the papel picado backdrop does on the Viva La Bonita shot.

Technique. Back: spot screen print, 11 colors plus a Cream underbase (Light Sky, Salt Pink, Light Pink, Sego Lily, Sage, Meadow, Forest, Aspen Gold, Terracotta, Rodeo Red, Mountain Navy, Ink line), flat, no halftones, so it feels like card stock and not a photo. Front: the single card, same separations. Wordmark under the board in the lotería serif. If the shop caps at eight heads, drop Light Pink, Sage and Forest into their neighbors; the illustrator decides which.

Placement and size. Back board 11 in wide x 10.8 in tall, top of board 3 in below the collar; LOTERÍA SALT LAKE at 0.4 in cap height, 0.75 in under the board. Front card 3.4 x 5.1 in on the wearer's left chest, top 3 in below the collar. Cards in the paper line at 2.4 x 3.6 in.

Colorways. Ink #212121 body, full brand card palette on a Cream underbase. No off-palette hit needed.

Estimated unit cost, 50-unit test run. Lane one, but the expensive end of it. Twelve screens for the back and the same films reused for the chest at $25 to $35 a screen is $300 to $420 amortized over 50, so $6 to $8 per shirt before the print itself; a 12-color back plus a 12-color chest at 50 pieces runs $12 to $16; blank $9 to $12; label $1.50 to $2. $28 to $38 landed. Retail $60 to $70. The card set, 50 boxed decks on a short offset run, lands at $9 to $14 each and retails $24 to $28. The honest note: the tee is cheaper per unit at 150 pieces than at 50, because the screens are the cost; if the test run is only 50, print the chest card as a single-color Cream line version and keep the full palette on the back.

One thing to verify before sampling. A wet-on-wet test of the twelve spot colors on the Cream underbase on garment-dyed black: whether Sego Lily and Light Pink hold their value over the underbase or need a second hit, because that decides whether the print feels like card stock or like a photo transfer.

Who finishes it. A Salt Lake County illustrator redraws all six in a lotería hand. The drawings in the SVG are blocking: composition, color placement, what is in each frame, the numbers. The misregistration and the hatching are kept on purpose. Second drop: El Lowrider, La Tejana, La Arepa.

What a local would say. "Where's El Lowrider?" (Second drop. Tell them.)

Risk. Lotería is the most-borrowed Mexican visual there is and "Lotería [City]" tees exist for a dozen cities. The numbers, the specific objects and a community illustrator's hand are what keep it off the airport shelf. If the illustrator is not from here, cut it.
